title: Factors Influencing Retrieval
summary: Why list position, the place you learned something, smells, and your internal state at learning all change how well you can retrieve it later.

lesson.title: Where and when you learned it
lesson.hook: You walk into your room to fetch something, and the moment you arrive, you forget what it was. Walk back to the parlour, and it pops back. Your memory was waiting in the other room.

slides.heading: Serial position, revisited
slides.body:
Meet twelve people at a party and you will likely remember the **first few** and the **last one or two** names, but lose the middle. This is the **serial position effect**: in a sequence, recall is better at the **beginning** and **end** than in the **middle**.

The early items benefit from the **primacy effect**, the late items from the **recency effect**.

slides.heading: Why the middle is lost
slides.body:
**Early items** are recalled because they have already been moved into **long-term memory**. **Late items** have an even better chance because they are **still in short-term memory**.

**Middle items** fall into a gap: they have **left short-term memory** but **not yet reached long-term memory**. Postman and Phillips (1965) saw this pattern as strong support for **separate short-term and long-term systems**.

slides.question: Middle items in a list are recalled poorly mainly because they:
options: Have left short-term memory but not yet reached long-term memory
slides.why: Middle items miss both benefits: they are no longer held in STM and were not rehearsed enough to reach LTM.

slides.heading: Context is encoded too
slides.body:
**Tulving and Thomson (1973)** proposed that features of the **setting** where you learn get **stored together with** what you learn, so the setting becomes a piece of the memory itself. This is the **encoding specificity principle**.

Return to the original context, or part of it, and it acts as a **retrieval cue**. Even **imagining** yourself back in that place can help (Smith et al., 1978).

slides.heading: The divers study
slides.body:
**Godden and Baddeley (1975)** had members of a university diving club learn word lists either **on land** or about **10 feet underwater**, then recall them in the **same** or the **other** setting.

Words learned underwater were best recalled underwater; words learned on land, best on land. When learning and recall contexts **matched**, scores were about **47% higher** than when they differed.

visual.label: Same context for learning and recall

slides.question: In Godden and Baddeley's study, divers who learned words underwater recalled them best:
slides.why: Recall was best when the recall context matched the learning context, here underwater.

slides.heading: People and smells as context
slides.body:
Context includes **people**. In a study by Bjorklund and colleagues (2000), participants interviewed twice about videos remembered more when the **same interviewer** questioned them both times.

It includes **smells**. Morgan (1996) exposed people to 40 words in a cubicle. Those who had a **pleasant odour** both while learning and at a surprise test five days later recalled significantly more words.

slides.heading: Studying in the exam hall
slides.story: Funke usually studies in her hostel room with music. Before her final exam, she spends two evenings revising in the empty lecture theatre where the exam will be held. During the paper, when a definition escapes her, she glances at the same windows and benches, pictures her revision evening, and the answer returns.
slides.takeaway: Reinstating the learning context, physically or in imagination, provides retrieval cues.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'define context-dependent memory' and the divers study, often with the 47% figure. Do not mix it up with state-dependent memory: context is the external setting; state is your internal condition. Also know why middle items are lost and who said the serial position effect supports separate stores.
slides.sampleQuestion: Godden and Baddeley (1975) demonstrated: (a) state-dependent memory with alcohol (b) context-dependent memory with divers (c) the recency effect with delays (d) dual coding with pictures
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b). In an essay, describe the design (land versus underwater, same versus different recall setting) and the result, then link to encoding specificity.

points: Serial position: first and last items recalled best.
Middle items have left STM but not reached LTM.
Encoding specificity: context is stored with the memory.
Godden and Baddeley: matching context gave about 47% better recall.
People, rooms and smells can all serve as context cues.

questions.stem: Recalling information better in the same physical setting where it was learned is called:
questions.explanation: Context-dependent memory concerns the external setting; state-dependent memory concerns internal state.

questions.stem: The divers study of context-dependent memory was carried out by:
questions.explanation: Godden and Baddeley (1975) used divers learning on land or underwater.

questions.stem: In the serial position effect, the poorest recall is for items:
questions.explanation: Middle items benefit from neither primacy nor recency.

questions.stem: The encoding specificity principle states that:
options: Memory is stored in one brain area
Features of the learning context are encoded with the information
questions.explanation: Tulving and Thomson (1973) argued that context becomes part of the memory trace.

questions.stem: Postman and Phillips (1965) argued that the serial position effect supports:
options: Separate short-term and long-term memory systems
questions.explanation: Different explanations for primacy and recency point to two separate stores.

questions.stem: In Godden and Baddeley's study, matching learning and recall contexts improved recall by about:
questions.explanation: Scores were roughly 47% higher when contexts matched.

questions.stem: Ike forgets what he went to the kitchen for, then remembers on returning to the sitting room. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Returning to the original setting supplied the cues that were encoded with the intention.

questions.stem: Students who smell the same perfume while studying and during a test recall more. This fits the findings of:
questions.explanation: Morgan found a pleasant odour present at both learning and testing improved recall.

questions.stem: A witness interviewed twice remembers more when the same police officer conducts both interviews. This matches:
questions.explanation: Bjorklund and colleagues found better recall with the same interviewer, treating the person as part of the context.

questions.stem: A student cannot sit the exam in the room where she studied. The best evidence-based tip is to:
options: Mentally picture herself in her study room
Study in many rooms at the last minute
questions.explanation: Smith et al. (1978) found that imagining the learning context can aid recall.

questions.stem: All of the following can serve as context cues EXCEPT:
options: A random setting never linked to the learning
The person who asked the questions
questions.explanation: A setting unrelated to the learning was never encoded with it, so it cannot cue the memory.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Middle items: left STM, not yet in LTM
Primacy: items still in short-term memory
Recency: items already in long-term memory
questions.explanation: Middle items are lost from STM before reaching LTM. Primacy reflects LTM; recency reflects STM.

questions.stem: I. Words learned underwater are best recalled on land. II. Context is encoded along with information. III. Imagining the learning context can help recall. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: II and III are correct. I is reversed: underwater words were best recalled underwater.

questions.stem: In the divers study, which condition produced the WORST recall?
options: Learn on land, recall on land
questions.explanation: Mismatched contexts gave lower recall than matched ones. Both matched conditions did better.

questions.stem: A researcher finds that recall is best when learning and testing happen in the same room, even when participants did not try to memorise the room. This supports the idea that context encoding is:
questions.explanation: Context gets encoded even without intention, as in Morgan's incidental-learning odour study.

lesson.title: Your inner state is a cue
lesson.hook: Can drinking coffee before both revision and the exam actually help you remember? Strangely, matching how you feel inside can matter as much as matching the room.

slides.heading: State-dependent memory
slides.body:
The **external** setting is not the only cue. Your **internal state** at learning is encoded too.

The **state-dependent memory effect** is the tendency to recall information better when you are in the **same internal state**, psychological or drug-induced, as when you encoded it.

slides.heading: Drugs and alcohol
slides.body:
State-dependent effects have been shown with **alcohol**, and with **marijuana**, **amphetamines** and **barbiturates** (Eich, 1980). People learned material **sober or intoxicated** and were tested in the same or the opposite state.

Recall was **best when the states matched** (Weingartner et al., 1976). Note: the effect appeared for **recall but not recognition**. Recognition gives its own strong cues, so it needs the internal state less.

slides.question: State-dependent effects for alcohol and drugs were found for:
slides.why: Recognition provides strong cues of its own, so the internal state matters less; the effect shows in recall.

slides.heading: Mood: weaker evidence
slides.body:
Does being in the **same happy or sad mood** at learning and recall help? Research has **not shown this conclusively**.

But **anxiety and fear** do affect memory. People under major life stress, such as bereavement, job loss or divorce, do **worse on tests of recent memory**. And students who learned words with **spiders or snakes** nearby recalled more when the creatures were **present again** at test (Lang et al., 2001).

slides.heading: Depression and memory
slides.body:
Clinically depressed adults tend to recall **more negative life events** (Clark & Teasdale, 1982) and to remember their parents as **unloving and rejecting** (Lewinsohn & Rosenbaum, 1987).

A meta-analysis of 48 studies found a significant link between **depression and memory impairment**, stronger in **younger** than older patients (Burt et al., 1995). Encouragingly, as depression **lifts**, negative recall and memory problems **reverse**.

slides.heading: The exam-hall nerves
slides.story: Chuka revises calmly at home, but on exam day his heart races and his hands shake. Material he knew well seems to vanish. His friend Rahila, who practised past questions under a timer to feel the pressure, finds exam-day nerves feel familiar, and her recall holds.
slides.takeaway: Matching your internal state, including arousal, at learning and testing can protect recall.

slides.question: Research on depression and memory shows that as depression lifts:
options: Negative recall and memory problems tend to reverse
slides.why: The memory effects of depression are linked to the state and tend to reverse as it improves.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: The classic trap: the manual's summary blurs context and state, but your lecturer will not. Context is outside you; state is inside you. Expect 'state-dependent effects appear for recall but not ___' (recognition), and depression findings with names. Remember the mood-matching evidence is inconclusive, while fear and anxiety effects are clearer.
slides.sampleQuestion: A student learns while slightly drunk and recalls best when slightly drunk again. This illustrates: (a) context-dependent memory (b) state-dependent memory (c) the primacy effect (d) encoding failure
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b): the match is in internal (pharmacological) state. Add that the effect appears in recall, not recognition (Weingartner et al., 1976).

points: State-dependent memory: recall is best in the same internal state as learning.
Shown for alcohol and drugs, for recall but not recognition.
Mood matching is not conclusively supported; fear and anxiety do affect memory.
Depression brings negative recall and memory impairment, worse in younger patients.
These effects reverse as depression lifts.

questions.stem: Recalling information better when in the same internal state as during learning is called:
questions.explanation: Matching internal (psychological or drug) state is state-dependent memory.

questions.stem: Clinically depressed adults tend to recall:
questions.explanation: Clark and Teasdale (1982) found depressed people recall more negative experiences.

questions.stem: Which of these is an internal state rather than an external context?
questions.explanation: Intoxication is an internal pharmacological state; the others are external context.

questions.stem: Eich (1980) reported state-dependent memory effects for all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Room temperature is an external feature; the drugs listed alter internal state.

questions.stem: Evidence that being in the same happy or sad mood at learning and recall helps memory is:
questions.explanation: Mood-matching effects have not been shown conclusively, though fear and anxiety do affect memory.

questions.stem: Burt and colleagues' (1995) meta-analysis found memory impairment in depression was greater in:
questions.explanation: Younger depressed patients showed more impairment of both recall and recognition than older ones.

questions.stem: Students learn words with snakes nearby, then recall more when the snakes are present again. This study by Lang and colleagues shows that:
options: Matching a fear state can aid recall
Fear has no effect on memory
questions.explanation: The fear-arousing creatures at both learning and test matched the internal state and aided recall.

questions.stem: Ngozi, recently bereaved, struggles to remember what she read yesterday. This is consistent with findings that:
questions.explanation: Significant life stress is linked with poorer performance on tests of recent memory.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from depression starts recalling more positive childhood memories. This fits the finding that:
options: Negative recall reverses as depression lifts
questions.explanation: As depression lifts, the negative recall bias and impairments tend to reverse.

questions.stem: Why was the state-dependent effect found for recall but not recognition?
options: Recognition supplies strong cues, reducing reliance on internal state
questions.explanation: With the answer present, recognition has strong external cues, so internal state matters less.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Clark & Teasdale (1982): parents remembered as rejecting
Lewinsohn & Rosenbaum (1987): parents remembered as rejecting
questions.explanation: Lewinsohn and Rosenbaum found depressed people recall parents as unloving. Clark and Teasdale found more negative recall generally.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes context-dependent from state-dependent memory?
options: Context concerns external setting; state concerns internal condition
Context concerns drugs; state concerns rooms
questions.explanation: Context is external (room, smell); state is internal (mood, drugs, arousal).

questions.stem: I. State-dependent effects appear for recall. II. They also appear strongly for recognition. III. Mood matching is conclusively supported. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: Only I is correct. The effect is weak or absent for recognition, and mood-matching evidence is not conclusive.

questions.stem: A student always revises after strong coffee but sits exams without it. Based on state-dependent memory, which prediction is most reasonable?
options: Essay (recall) answers may suffer more than multiple-choice answers
questions.explanation: A state mismatch mainly hurts recall; recognition is less affected because it offers its own cues.

questions.stem: Two groups learn words sober. One is tested sober, the other intoxicated. A third group learns and is tested intoxicated. Which group should recall worst?
questions.explanation: The mismatched group lacks the state cue. Intoxication also generally impairs encoding, but matched states still beat mismatched ones.
